exercises.approach: Walk the four times in order, multiplying survival by one minus events over the number at risk at each event time.
exercises.why: At time 1, 4 are at risk and 1 fails, giving 3/4. The censor at time 2 removes one record without a drop. At time 3, 2 remain and 1 fails, giving 3/4 times 1/2 = 3/8. At time 4 the last record fails, giving 0.
exercises.wrong: Dividing events by the original 4 at every step. That gives 3/4, then 2/4 and 1/4, which ignores that the censored record had already left the risk set.

exercises.approach: Copy the data, set only `event[2]` to 1, refit, and read survival at time 2.
exercises.why: As an event, time 2 has 3 at risk and 1 failure, so survival falls to 3/4 times 2/3 = 1/2. The same times now answer a different question because the coding changed what counts as failure.
exercises.wrong: Treating censoring as a detail that barely moves the curve. Here it moves survival at time 2 from 0.75 to 0.5, and at time 3 from 0.375 to 0.25.

exercises.approach: Check that the event column has no NA and contains only 0 and 1 before building Surv.
exercises.why: This lesson defines 1 as an observed event and 0 as censored. Any other value, such as the 2 in c(0, 2), cannot be read under that contract, so the validator stops.
exercises.wrong: Passing the column straight to Surv. Surv also accepts 1/2 coding, in which 1 means censored, so a column of 1s and 2s would be read with a meaning the lesson never declared.

exercises.approach: Fit coxph on the 12 record fixture, take coef(fit) as the log hazard ratio for group 1 against group 0, and exponentiate it.
exercises.why: Group 0 has 5 events in 6 records and group 1 has 3 events with 3 censors. Solving the partial likelihood by hand gives a coefficient near -0.56 and a hazard ratio near 0.57, with a standard error near 0.74, so the data also fit a ratio of 1.
exercises.wrong: Reading 0.57 as group 1's survival probability relative to group 0's. It compares instantaneous event rates among those still at risk, and the survival curves differ by a nonconstant amount.
exercises.verify: `all(is.finite(coef(fit)))` returns TRUE, and `exp(coef(fit))` returns a single positive value near 0.57.

exercises.approach: Run cox.zph on the fit and read the group and GLOBAL rows as a diagnostic with stated limits.
exercises.why: The test asks whether scaled Schoenfeld residuals drift with time. With 8 events in 12 records it has little power, so a large p value only says that no drift was detected here.
exercises.wrong: Writing that proportional hazards is proven because p is above 0.05. A sample this small would also miss many real violations, so absence of evidence is all it shows.
exercises.verify: `all(is.finite(diagnostic$table))` returns TRUE and `"GLOBAL" %in% rownames(diagnostic$table)` returns TRUE.

exercises.approach: Keep the censored record in the analysis so it contributes to every risk set until time 2.
exercises.why: In the four record fixture the record censored at time 2 survived past time 1, so it belongs in the denominator at time 1. Kaplan-Meier uses that partial exposure; a plain average of event times cannot.
exercises.wrong: Dropping the censored row and averaging 1, 3 and 4 to get about 2.67. The curve on the remaining 3 rows becomes 2/3, 1/3 and 0, lower than 3/4, 3/8 and 0, because a known survivor vanished.
exercises.verify: `sum(d$event)` returns 3 against `nrow(d)` of 4, which shows one record would be lost by dropping censored rows.
